summary.text: Ephesus stood near the mouth of the Cayster river, on the slopes of two hills, Prion and Coressus, about three miles from the Aegean coast opposite the island of Samos. An artificial harbor with a sea channel, and roads running inland, made Ephesus the most easily reached city in the province of Asia, by both land and sea. The city's greatest landmark was the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world: a temple open to the sky, about 425 feet long, ringed by 127 columns 60 feet high. Acts records the Ephesians' own pride in guarding this temple, calling their city "temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis."

history.text: According to Acts, Paul spent about three years in Ephesus, reasoning daily in a lecture hall called the school of Tyrannus. When his preaching hurt the business of craftsmen who made silver shrines of Artemis, the silversmith Demetrius stirred up a riot: a crowd dragged two of Paul's companions into the city's great theatre and shouted for two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" Paul's letter to the Ephesians is addressed to believers in the city; 1 and 2 Timothy also mention Ephesus, and it is the first of the seven churches addressed in Revelation.

In the second century AD, long after Paul's time, Ephesus gained some of the grand buildings seen there today, including the Library of Celsus, built as a tomb and library for the Roman senator Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus. Pilgrims from across the Mediterranean had once come to the Temple of Artemis; from the fifth century, Christian pilgrims came instead to the Church of Mary and the Basilica of St. John.

Today the ruins of Ephesus, near the Turkish town of Selçuk, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Visitors walk its old processional way past the Library of Celsus and the Great Theatre, though little remains of the Temple of Artemis itself.
